hook: a demon general undone by one syllable, and Kali springing from the goddess's frowning brow

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Devi Mahatmya, the gods bowed to the goddess who lives in all beings, even as hunger and error, and she answered Shumbha's proposal with a vow. Did you notice a hunger without scolding it? Day one thousand sixty-eight.

One syllable. Hum. That's all it takes in the sixth chapter. Shumbha, furious at the goddess's vow, sends a general named Dhumralochana with an army and an order: drag her here by the hair. The general reaches the mountain and shouts at her to come quietly. The goddess answers, in paraphrase: you're strong, and you've brought an army. If you take me by force, what can I do? He rushes at her. And she makes one sound, hum, and he's burned to ash. Her lion takes care of the army. The last day of the first week of year four, and the goddess is about to show a face the story hasn't shown yet.
screen: `DRAG HER HERE BY THE HAIR.` → `ONE SOUND: HUM.` → `A FACE NOT SEEN YET.`

segments.voice: In the seventh chapter Shumbha sends Chanda and Munda, the two servants who first told him about her, with a bigger army. They find the goddess seated on her lion on a golden peak of the mountain, smiling. They come at her with bows and swords. And her face goes dark with anger, dark as ink. Then, from her frowning forehead, another goddess springs out. The text describes her plainly and without softening. Kali. Dark, with a gaping mouth and a lolling tongue. Thin, wrapped in a tiger skin, wearing a garland of human heads, a skull-topped staff and a sword in her hands. She fills the sky with her roar. She tears into the army, swallowing elephants whole with their riders and their bells, crunching chariots in her teeth. She seizes Chanda by the hair and cuts off his head, then Munda. She carries the two heads back to the goddess, laughing, and offers them as a gift. And the goddess gives her a name: because you've brought me Chanda and Munda, you'll be known as Chamunda. Look at where Kali comes from in this text. Not from outside. From the goddess's own brow, at the moment the threat comes close. The same goddess who smiled on the mountain carries this fierce face inside her. Now look back at the week. A king and a merchant in a forest, unable to let go. Vishnu's sleep, and two demons outwitted. Every god's gift, and a lion. A shape-shifter pinned. A hymn about kindness to enemies. A refrain to the goddess in all beings. And now Kali. One goddess, seen from more and more sides.
screen: `HER FACE GOES DARK AS INK.` · `KALI SPRINGS FROM HER BROW.` · `CHANDA AND MUNDA: CHAMUNDA.` · `THE WEEK: ONE GODDESS, MANY SIDES.` · then, large: `THE FIERCE FACE WAS INSIDE HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the smile and the fierce face. Sit tall, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone or something you would stand up for. Picture them threatened, just for a moment, and notice whatever rises in the body: maybe a straightening of the back, a firmness in the jaw, maybe something else. Don't act on it. Let it be strength, not cruelty. Then let the calm come back alongside it, breath by breath, the way the goddess on the mountain was smiling and fierce at once. If you pray, you can bow to the goddess, or to God, in the words you already use. If you don't, let the breath hold both. The bell holds the time.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its sixth and seventh chapters: one syllable that burns a general to ash, and Kali, springing from the goddess's own brow, named Chamunda.

Your line: the Devi Mahatmya, read whole. Today, if something you care about needs protecting, stand up for it once, firmly and without cruelty. Day one thousand sixty-eight. Week one of year four, done.

howItsDone: Kali and Chamunda are worshiped in Hindu temples, and the seventh chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, where Kali springs from the goddess's brow and is named Chamunda, is recited as part of the whole text.

fork.setup: you're the goddess. Chanda and Munda come at you with a huge army, bows drawn. what happens?
options: you call the gods for help.
your face darkens, and Kali springs from your brow.
fork.reveal: her face goes dark as ink with anger, and Kali springs from her forehead, destroys the army, and brings back Chanda's and Munda's heads.

original.note: Sanskrit: Cāmuṇḍā, the name the goddess gives Kali for killing Chanda and Munda.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kali is a separate, frightening goddess.
what it means: in the Devi Mahatmya, Kali springs from the goddess's own brow when danger comes close, and is named Chamunda.
what a scholar hears: chapter 7, where Kālī emerges from Ambikā's forehead (lalāṭa) and the name Cāmuṇḍā is explained from Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 7 (Kali; Chanda and Munda; the name Chamunda)

notes: Last day of week one of year four; looks back over 1062–1067. Covers chapters 6 and 7.

Chapter 6 paraphrased: Dhumralochana sent with an army to drag the goddess by the hair; her reply (if you take me by force, what can I do to you?); reduced to ashes by the sound hum (huṃkāra); the lion destroys the army. The army's size is given in the text and deliberately not spoken. 'Smoke-Eye' renders the name; confirm.

Chapter 7 paraphrased: Chanda and Munda find her smiling on her lion on a golden peak of the Himalaya; her face becomes dark as ink; Kali emerges from her forehead with sword and noose, skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), garland of heads, tiger skin, emaciated, gaping mouth, lolling tongue, red eyes; she devours elephants with riders and bells, crushes chariots; kills Chanda and Munda; offers the heads; the goddess names her Chamunda. Confirm.
Kali's appearance is described plainly, as the text does. Confirm the tone suits the path and that a Keeper from a Shakta lineage would recognize her.
howItsDone kept general ('worshiped in Hindu temples'); confirm.
